title: Reading Time: 6 minutes
text:
Reading Time: 6 minutes

Many people with Crohn's disease experience symptoms for months or even years before receiving a confirmed diagnosis. This delay is not unusual, and understanding why it happens can help set realistic expectations during what is often a frustrating and uncertain time.

## Why a diagnosis can take time

Crohn's disease does not present with a single defining test or symptom. It is a chronic inflammatory condition that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, from mouth to anus, though it most commonly involves the end of the small intestine and the beginning of the colon. Because inflammation can occur in patches and vary in severity, the clinical picture differs considerably between individuals.

Symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhoea, fatigue, and weight loss overlap with numerous other conditions, including irritable bowel syndrome, coeliac disease, infections, and other forms of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) such as ulcerative colitis. Doctors must carefully rule out other causes before confirming a Crohn's diagnosis.

Additionally, some people experience periods where symptoms improve or disappear entirely, making it harder to recognise a pattern or justify further investigation. Blood tests, imaging, and endoscopy are often needed to build a complete picture, and these investigations take time to arrange and interpret.

## The diagnostic process

Diagnosis typically begins with a detailed history and physical examination. Your doctor will ask about the duration, frequency, and nature of your symptoms, as well as any family history of IBD, recent travel, or medication use.

Blood tests are usually performed early. These may include markers of inflammation such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), as well as full blood counts to check for anaemia or signs of infection. Faecal calprotectin, a protein released by white blood cells in the gut, is often measured in stool samples to help distinguish between inflammatory and non-inflammatory bowel conditions. Elevated levels suggest inflammation, though they do not specify the cause.

Imaging studies such as MRI or CT scans may be used to visualise the bowel structure and identify areas of thickening, narrowing, or inflammation. These scans are particularly useful for assessing the small intestine, which is difficult to reach with standard endoscopy.

Endoscopy, including colonoscopy and sometimes upper endoscopy, allows direct visualisation of the bowel lining and the opportunity to take biopsies. Biopsies are small tissue samples examined under a microscope to look for characteristic features of Crohn's disease, such as granulomas (clusters of immune cells), patchy inflammation, and changes to the gut lining structure. These findings, combined with clinical symptoms and other test results, form the basis of a Crohn's diagnosis.

## What makes Crohn's disease difficult to identify

Crohn's disease is defined by patchy inflammation that may be present in one section whilst adjacent areas appear completely normal. This means investigations might miss affected areas, leading to inconclusive results. In such cases, repeat tests or additional imaging may be necessary.

Symptoms can also fluctuate. Some people experience active flares with obvious symptoms, followed by periods of remission where symptoms lessen or resolve. If investigations are performed during a quieter phase, inflammation may be less apparent, making definitive diagnosis harder.

## What to expect during the waiting period

The time between your first symptoms and a diagnosis can feel uncertain, but a careful, step-by-step approach is how your team makes sure they reach the right diagnosis and choose the treatment that suits you.

Keeping a simple symptom diary during this time can really help. Noting things like how often you're going to the toilet, any pain or fatigue, and possible triggers gives your healthcare team useful information and can reveal patterns that might not come up in a single appointment.

Continue seeking medical advice if symptoms persist or worsen, even if initial tests have been normal. Repeat investigations may reveal changes that were not present earlier.

## Moving forward after diagnosis

Once diagnosis is confirmed, treatment can begin. The aim of treatment in Crohn's disease is to reduce inflammation, manage symptoms, and prevent complications. This typically involves medications such as aminosalicylates, commonly known as (5-ASAs), corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, or biologic therapies, depending on the severity and location of disease.

Diagnosis also opens the door to specialist support, including access to gastroenterologists, IBD nurses, and dietitians who understand the condition and can provide tailored advice. Regular monitoring through blood tests, imaging, and endoscopy helps assess disease activity and adjust treatment as needed.

Whilst a diagnosis of Crohn's disease is a significant moment, it also brings clarity and a path forward. Understanding the condition, its triggers, and how it responds to treatment allows for more informed decisions and better long-term management.

## Practical takeaways

• Keep a detailed symptom diary, including bowel habits, pain, fatigue, and any foods or stressors that seem to worsen symptoms.

• Do not hesitate to seek further medical advice if symptoms persist or worsen, even if earlier tests were inconclusive.

• Ask your healthcare team to explain test results and the reasoning behind each investigation, so you understand what is being ruled in or out.

• If you have a family history of IBD, mention this to your doctor, as it may influence the diagnostic approach.

• Be patient with the process. Diagnosis takes time because accuracy is essential for effective treatment.

• Once diagnosed, engage with specialist services and ask about monitoring strategies to help manage the condition over time.

## Conclusion

Getting a Crohn's diagnosis can take time, often because Crohn's can look like other conditions, and your medical team will want a clear picture before starting treatment. Waiting for answers isn't easy, but a careful process means the treatment you're offered is the right fit for you. And once you have your diagnosis, you won't be left to manage alone: regular check-ins with your team help keep your symptoms under control and support your health over the long term.

title: Reading Time: 5 minutes
text:
Reading Time: 5 minutes

The similarity in abbreviations has led to countless misunderstandings, both in casual conversation and in healthcare settings. If  you've mixed them up, you're in good company; even healthcare professionals sometimes do a double-take. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) are actually quite different conditions, with distinct causes, ways of being diagnosed, and treatment approaches. Understanding why they are so often confused, and what truly separates them, matters for anyone navigating digestive symptoms or seeking a clear diagnosis.

## What IBD and IBS actually are

Inflammatory bowel disease is an umbrella term for chronic conditions where the immune system triggers ongoing inflammation in the gut. Think of it as the body's defences accidentally attacking the digestive tract. The two main types are Crohn's disease, which can affect any part of the digestive tract, and ulcerative colitis, which is limited to the colon and rectum. IBD involves measurable inflammation that doctors can see through endoscopy (a camera examination of the gut), imaging scans, and straightforward blood and stool tests.

Irritable bowel syndrome, by contrast, is what doctors call a 'functional' condition. This means that the gut behaves differently, even though it looks structurally normal. It can cause real and often distressing symptoms, including abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits, but without detectable structural damage or inflammation on standard tests. IBS is diagnosed based on symptom patterns and the exclusion of other conditions, rather than through direct observation of tissue changes.

## Why the confusion happens

The overlap begins with symptoms. Both conditions can present with abdominal pain, diarrhoea, urgency, and fatigue. A person experiencing these for the first time has no way of knowing whether the underlying cause is inflammatory or functional. Even healthcare professionals may initially consider both possibilities during early assessment.

The abbreviations themselves compound the problem. Three letters, two of which are identical, separated by a single vowel. In spoken conversation, especially over the phone or in noisy environments, IBD and IBS can sound virtually identical. Patients are sometimes told they have one condition, only to later realise the diagnosis was the other.

There is also a widespread lack of public awareness. IBD remains less well known than many other chronic diseases, and IBS is often misunderstood. This creates an information gap where assumptions fill the space that clear knowledge should occupy.

## The critical differences

The most important distinction lies in the presence or absence of inflammation. In IBD, the immune system is overactive, producing inflammatory cytokines (chemical messengers released by immune cells) that irritate and damage the gut lining over time. This is why treatment and monitoring matter. Catching and managing the inflammation early helps prevent it from causing lasting problems.

IBS does not involve this type of immune-driven tissue damage. It cannot turn into IBD, and having IBS does not increase the risk of developing IBD. They are separate conditions.

Diagnosis reflects this difference. IBD is confirmed through endoscopy with biopsies, imaging such as MRI or CT enterography, and blood or stool tests showing active inflammation. IBS is typically diagnosed using internationally agreed criteria (known as the Rome IV guidelines) that look at the pattern and duration of symptoms in the absence of certain warning signs like weight loss, rectal bleeding, or symptoms that regularly wake you up at night.

Treatment approaches diverge accordingly. IBD is managed with medicines that reduce inflammation or calm down the immune system, ranging from anti-inflammatory tablets (such as aminosalicylates, or ASAs) and steroids (corticosteroids) to more targeted therapies for moderate or severe disease (for example, immunomodulators and biologic therapies). Diet also plays a supporting role, particularly focusing on strengthening the lining of the gut and making sure key nutrients aren't being lost. IBS management centres on symptom relief through dietary modification, such as the low FODMAP diet, alongside approaches that target the gut-brain connection. This can include techniques like cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and, in some cases, medicines that target bowel motility or gut sensitivity.

## When the two overlap

Complicating matters further, some people with IBD also experience IBS-like symptoms. This can occur even when inflammation is well controlled or in remission. In these cases, the gut may have become more sensitive due to prior inflammation, leading to symptoms such as bloating or discomfort without active disease.

This overlap can make it difficult to distinguish between a flare of IBD and functional symptoms. Clinicians rely on objective markers, such as faecal calprotectin or endoscopic assessment, to clarify whether inflammation has returned or whether symptoms are functional. Treating these situations requires a nuanced approach that addresses both inflammatory control and symptom management.

## Why accurate diagnosis matters

Getting the right diagnosis makes a real difference. Someone with IBD who is correctly identified early can start the right treatment sooner, which helps protect the gut and maintain quality of life. Equally, someone with IBS who knows their diagnosis can focus on the approaches that actually work for their condition, rather than going through tests or treatments that are not relevant.

For patients, clarity about the diagnosis informs decision-making, treatment expectations, and a clearer understanding of what to expect long term. IBD is a lifelong condition that requires ongoing monitoring and, in many cases, sustained medical therapy. IBS, whilst chronic and often challenging, does not carry the same risks of structural complications or the need for immunosuppressive treatment.

## Practical Takeaways

•	Keep a symptom diary. Note when symptoms happen, what they feel like, and anything that seems to trigger them. If you notice blood in the stool or unintended weight loss, make sure to flag that to your doctor.
•	Do not hesitate to ask your healthcare team to clearly explain your diagnosis and what it means for you. If anything is unclear, asking questions is always the right thing to do.
•	If you have been diagnosed with IBS but notice new symptoms like persistent bleeding, unexplained weight loss, or symptoms that regularly wake you at night, it is worth going back to your doctor for a review.
•	Trust the process, but stay engaged. If symptoms persist or change, let your doctor know. Investigations can be repeated or extended if needed.
•	Remember that both conditions are manageable, and a diagnosis, even if it takes a little time to get right, is the starting point for getting the right support.

## Conclusion

IBD and IBS may share a similar acronym and some surface-level symptoms, but they are distinct in cause, diagnosis, and treatment. The confusion between them is understandable, but not inevitable. Clear communication, access to appropriate diagnostic testing, and patient education all play a role in reducing misunderstanding. Navigating digestive symptoms is not always straightforward, and it is okay if it takes time to get clarity. What matters is that you feel informed, supported, and confident asking questions.

title: Reading Time: 5 minutes
text:
Reading Time: 5 minutes

If you have been diagnosed with Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, you may already know that both sit under the umbrella of inflammatory bowel disease, or IBD. Both involve inflammation in the digestive tract, but they are actually quite different conditions. Knowing how they differ can help you make sense of your diagnosis, your symptoms, and why your care might look different from someone else with IBD.

## What exactly is IBD?

Inflammatory bowel disease is a term used to describe conditions where the gut becomes inflamed on a long-term basis. The two main types are Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. In both, the immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of the gut, causing ongoing irritation and inflammation. The key differences come down to where that inflammation happens and how deeply it goes. 

## Where does the inflammation happen?

This is one of the clearest differences between the two. Ulcerative colitis only affects the colon, also known as the large intestine. The inflammation is continuous, usually starting in the rectum and spreading upward in an unbroken pattern. The amount affected can vary from person to person.

Crohn’s disease, on the other hand, can appear anywhere along the digestive tract from the mouth to the anus, though it most commonly affects the end of the small intestine and the start of the colon. Unlike ulcerative colitis, Crohn’s tends to appear in patches, with healthy stretches of gut sitting right next to inflamed ones.

## How deep does the inflammation go?

In ulcerative colitis, inflammation stays in the innermost lining of the bowel wall. In Crohn’s disease, it can go much deeper, sometimes all the way through the bowel wall. This deeper involvement can sometimes lead to narrowing in parts of the bowel or, in some cases, unusual connections forming between different parts of the gut. These are manageable complications that doctors regularly monitor for and treat.

## What are the symptom patterns?

There is a lot of overlap in symptoms, but each condition does tend to show up in slightly different ways. Both can cause abdominal pain, diarrhoea, fatigue, weight loss, and changes in bowel habits.

Ulcerative colitis often presents with bloody diarrhoea and an urgent need to use the toilet. Pain tends to be felt in the lower left abdomen, where the colon sits. Because inflammation stays in the colon, nutrient absorption (which mainly happens in the small intestine) is less likely to be affected.

Crohn’s symptoms depend on which part of the gut is involved. When the small intestine is affected, there may be cramping pain, often felt in the lower right abdomen. Diarrhoea is common but is less frequently bloody. Because the small intestine is responsible for absorbing nutrients, some people with Crohn’s may find it harder to get everything they need from food, particularly if a larger section is inflamed.

## What is happening inside the gut?

In both conditions, the immune system becomes overactive and starts attacking the lining of the gut, even though there is nothing harmful there. This triggers ongoing inflammation and can disrupt the balance of bacteria and other microorganisms living in the gut. The exact processes involved differ slightly between the two, which is partly why they can respond differently to certain treatments. Researchers have also found some genetic factors that can increase the likelihood of developing IBD, and while some of these are shared between Crohn’s and ulcerative colitis, others are specific to one condition.

## What should I consider long term?

People who have had ulcerative colitis for a number of years are usually offered regular colonoscopies as part of their routine care. These checks help doctors keep a close eye on the bowel and pick up any changes early. It is a reassuring part of long-term monitoring, not something to worry about.

It is important to keep an eye on nutrition as it is common to see deficiencies in vitamins and minerals, particularly iron, vitamin B12, and fat-soluble vitamins. A dietitian or gastroenterology team can help make sure nutrient levels stay where they should be.

Both conditions can occasionally cause symptoms outside the gut, such as joint pain or skin changes. These are known as extraintestinal manifestations and can occur in both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

## How are the conditions diagnosed?

Diagnosis involves a combination of  medical and family history, blood tests, stool tests, imaging, and a colonoscopy, which allows doctors to look directly at the bowel lining and take small samples for testing. In ulcerative colitis, the pattern of continuous inflammation starting from the rectum is usually visible. In Crohn’s, patchy inflammation and involvement of the small intestine may be seen. Certain microscopic features in the tissue samples can also help point toward one condition over the other. Diagnosis draws on the full picture rather than any single test.

## How are they treated?

Treatment for both conditions aims to reduce inflammation and keep symptoms under control. This can include anti-inflammatory medicines, medicines that calm the immune system, and in some cases, biologic therapies that target specific parts of the immune response. The right approach depends on where the disease is, how active it is, and how it responds over time.

Surgery is sometimes needed. For ulcerative colitis, removing the colon (known as a colectomy) can resolve the condition entirely, as it is confined to that organ. For Crohn’s, surgery can help manage specific problems but is not a cure, since inflammation can recur elsewhere in the digestive tract.

Nutrition plays an important role in both conditions, and dietary support can help manage symptoms and maintain wellbeing alongside medical treatment. Omega-3 fatty acids, particularly EPA, have been studied for their role in supporting healthy inflammatory processes in the gut.

## The bottom line

Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis are different conditions, but both are manageable with the right support. Understanding a little more about how they work can make it easier to have informed conversations with your care team and feel more in control of your health. If you have questions about your diagnosis, your gastroenterologist or IBD nurse is always the best place to start.

title: Crohn's disease vs. ulcerative colitis: what's actually the difference?
text:
# Crohn's disease vs. ulcerative colitis: what's actually the difference?
# Understanding the key differences between these two conditions

When someone receives a diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease, the next question is often whether it's Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis. Both conditions involve chronic inflammation of the digestive tract, both can cause similar symptoms, and both fall under the same umbrella term. Yet they are distinct conditions with different patterns of inflammation, different areas of involvement, and different implications for long-term management.

## What inflammatory bowel disease means

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) refers to a group of conditions characterised by persistent inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract. The two main forms are Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Both involve an inappropriate immune response in which the body's immune system attacks the lining of the gut, leading to inflammation, tissue damage, and a range of symptoms including abdominal pain, diarrhoea, fatigue, and weight loss. The inflammation in IBD is chronic, meaning it persists over time and typically requires ongoing management.

## Where the inflammation occurs

The most fundamental difference between Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis is the location and pattern of inflammation.

Ulcerative colitis affects only the colon (large intestine) and rectum. The inflammation begins in the rectum and extends continuously along the colon. It does not skip areas, meaning that if inflammation is present, it forms an unbroken stretch from the rectum upwards. The inflammation is also limited to the innermost layer of the bowel wall, known as the mucosa.

Crohn's disease, by contrast, can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, from the mouth to the anus. It most commonly involves the end of the small intestine (the terminal ileum) and the beginning of the colon, but it can appear anywhere. Unlike ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease causes patchy inflammation, meaning that areas of inflamed tissue are separated by sections of healthy tissue. This pattern is sometimes referred to as "skip lesions". Crohn's disease also affects the full thickness of the bowel wall, not just the surface layer.

## How the inflammation behaves

The depth and pattern of inflammation influence how each condition behaves and what complications may arise.

In ulcerative colitis, because the inflammation is confined to the mucosal layer, the primary issues relate to surface damage. This can lead to ulceration, bleeding, and an increased urgency to pass stools. The continuous nature of the inflammation means that once it reaches a certain point in the colon, everything from that point back to the rectum is involved.

In Crohn's disease, the transmural inflammation (affecting all layers of the bowel wall) can lead to complications such as strictures, where the bowel narrows due to scarring, and fistulas, which are abnormal connections that form between different parts of the bowel or between the bowel and other organs or the skin. These complications are rare in ulcerative colitis because the inflammation does not extend through the full thickness of the bowel wall.

## Symptoms and how they differ

Both conditions share common symptoms, including diarrhoea, abdominal pain, fatigue, and unintended weight loss. However, the specific presentation can vary.

Ulcerative colitis often causes bloody diarrhoea and a frequent, urgent need to pass stools, particularly when the rectum is inflamed. The blood is typically visible and mixed with the stool. Pain is often felt in the lower left side of the abdomen.

Crohn's disease may cause diarrhoea that is less likely to contain visible blood, though this can occur. Pain is more commonly felt in the lower right side of the abdomen, especially when the terminal ileum is involved. Because Crohn's can affect the small intestine, it may also interfere with nutrient absorption, leading to deficiencies in vitamins and minerals. Perianal symptoms, such as skin tags, fissures, or abscesses around the anus, are more common in Crohn's disease.

It is essential to note that symptoms do not always reflect the degree of inflammation present. Some people experience significant symptoms with mild inflammation, while others may have more extensive inflammation with relatively few symptoms.

## How the diagnosis is made

Diagnosing IBD and distinguishing between Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis involves a combination of clinical assessment, blood tests, stool tests, imaging, and endoscopy with biopsy.

Colonoscopy allows direct visualisation of the colon and terminal ileum, and biopsies taken during the procedure can show the depth and pattern of inflammation. In ulcerative colitis, the inflammation appears continuous and superficial. In Crohn's disease, the inflammation is patchy and extends deeper into the tissue.

Imaging techniques such as MRI or computed tomography (CT) scans are often used in Crohn's disease to assess the small intestine, which cannot be fully examined by colonoscopy. These scans can identify areas of thickening, strictures, or fistulas.

Blood tests may reveal markers of inflammation, such as C-reactive protein (CRP), and can help assess for anaemia or nutritional deficiencies. Stool tests, including faecal calprotectin, can indicate the presence of intestinal inflammation and help monitor disease activity over time.

## Treatment approaches and why they differ

Both conditions are managed with medicines that reduce inflammation and suppress the immune response. These include aminosalicylates (more commonly known as ASAs), corticosteroids, immunomodulators, and biologic therapies. The choice of treatment depends on the severity and location of the disease, as well as individual response.

ASAs are often used in mild to moderate ulcerative colitis and can be effective for maintaining remission. They are less commonly used in Crohn's disease, particularly when the small intestine is involved.

Biologic therapies, which target specific components of the immune response, are used in both conditions, particularly in moderate to severe disease or when other treatments have not been effective. These include anti-tumour necrosis factor (anti-TNF) agents and other targeted therapies.

Surgery may be required in both conditions, but the implications differ. In ulcerative colitis, removal of the colon (colectomy) can be curative, as the disease is confined to that organ. In Crohn's disease, surgery is not curative because the condition can recur in other parts of the gastrointestinal tract. Surgery in Crohn's disease is typically used to address complications such as strictures or fistulas.

## Why the distinction matters

Understanding whether someone has Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis is essential for guiding treatment, monitoring for complications, and planning long-term care. The two conditions have different risks, different patterns of progression, and different responses to treatment. Accurate diagnosis allows for a more tailored approach to managing inflammation, reducing symptoms, and maintaining quality of life.

## Conclusion

Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are both forms of inflammatory bowel disease, but they differ in where and how inflammation occurs, the complications that may arise, and the way they are managed. Ulcerative colitis is confined to the colon and affects only the inner lining, while Crohn's disease can occur anywhere in the digestive tract and involves the full thickness of the bowel wall. Recognising these differences is central to effective, individualised care.
